title: Coriander Prices Surge Past Rs 200 Per Kg as Heavy Rains Disrupt Indian Supply
excerpt: The humble dhaniya, once a free add-on with vegetable purchases, now commands premium retail prices of Rs 220-230 per kg in Delhi after floods damage crops in Nashik.
body:
• Retail coriander prices in Delhi have reached Rs 220-230 per kg, up from a typical wholesale rate of Rs 25 per kg
  • Heavy rainfall and flooding near Nashik, Maharashtra — a key coriander-growing region — damaged standing crops and disrupted transportation
  • Wholesale prices at Delhi's Azadpur mandi briefly surged to Rs 200 per kg before easing to about Rs 110 per kg
  • Supplies from backup sources including Karnataka and Bengaluru have been limited and of inferior quality

Dhaniya — the bunch of fresh coriander that vegetable vendors across India have traditionally tucked into shopping bags at no extra cost — has become an unexpectedly expensive kitchen essential. Retail prices for fresh coriander have surged past Rs 200 per kg in several markets, driven by heavy rainfall that has devastated crops in major growing regions.

What Is Driving the Price Spike

The sharp increase follows intense rainfall in and around Nashik in Maharashtra, one of India's primary sources of green coriander for markets across northern India. Flooding toward the end of July damaged standing crops and disrupted transportation networks, reducing the volume of coriander that could survive the long-distance journey to Delhi.

At Delhi's Azadpur mandi, one of Asia's largest wholesale fruit and vegetable markets, fresh coriander prices climbed to Rs 175 per kg at wholesale, according to an Economic Times report. Retail rates earlier this week touched Rs 220-230 per kg. Mukesh Kumar, a vegetable trader at Azadpur, said wholesale prices during this period are typically around Rs 25 per kg — making the current spike roughly a seven-fold increase.

"It is very difficult to predict prices of leafy greens during the rainy season as they can jump multi-fold within a day of delayed arrival."

— Aniket Kapadi, coriander trader, Nashik

A Supply Chain Under Strain

The supply crunch began building about a month before the most recent spike. Krushna Borade, a vegetable trader and exporter based in Nashik, told the Times of India that good-quality green coriander had already tightened locally, pushing Nashik prices to nearly Rs 130 per kg. Supplies from other producing centers, including Bengaluru and Latur, had also declined because of delayed rainfall in those regions.

The recent spell of heavy rain caused extensive damage to coriander crops across several regions, making premium-quality produce increasingly difficult to procure. The shortage has been particularly acute for varieties that can endure long-distance transportation.

Coriander harvested around Nashik is typically sent first to cold-storage facilities in Indore before being transported to Delhi, leaving the supply chain highly susceptible to rain-related interruptions at multiple points. Karnataka has helped bridge part of the shortfall, but arrivals have remained limited and the quality of produce has generally been inferior, according to traders.

Impact on Consumers and Vendors

The price surge has changed shopping behavior across Indian markets. Vendors report that customers who would normally buy a kilogram of vegetables are now purchasing only half a kilogram. Daily wage earners, who earn between Rs 150 and Rs 200 a day, have reduced vegetable purchases significantly.

The spike is not limited to coriander. Heavy monsoon rainfall has pushed up prices for other leafy greens including spinach and fenugreek (methi), with retailers across multiple states reporting 30% price increases. Tomato and capsicum prices have also risen sharply in rain-affected regions.

When Prices May Ease

Traders say prices are difficult to predict during monsoon season, as they can swing dramatically with each day of delayed arrivals. Wholesale rates at Azadpur have already eased from a peak of Rs 200 to about Rs 110 per kg, suggesting some stabilization. However, sustained improvement depends on weather conditions in growing regions over the coming weeks. If the heavy rain subsides and new supplies from Karnataka and other regions strengthen, prices could gradually return to more typical levels.
nri_angle: Coriander is a staple herb in Indian cooking worldwide, and the price surge affects diaspora members visiting India as well as the broader Indian food supply chain.
